title: Paul and women
hook: Paul names women co-workers, Junia, Phoebe, Prisca, and also wrote restrictions; churches read these differently
tomorrow: a letter mailed to Rome long ago: who is it addressed to now?

segments.voice: The household codes spoke into a Roman house and pushed on it: one to another, and a Master in heaven. Read in context. Now the women who show up in those same letters.
screen: `READ IN CONTEXT.` → `THE WOMEN IN THE LETTERS.`

segments.voice: At an awards show, the thank-yous are where you find out who actually did the work. Romans has a thank-you page. It's the last one, the easy one to skim, a list of hellos. And the first name on it is a woman's: "I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea." Paul is vouching for her to a church that hasn't met her. Some readers think she carried the letter itself.
screen: `THE THANK-YOUS TELL WHO DID THE WORK.` → `THE LAST PAGE OF ROMANS.` → `FIRST NAME: PHEBE.`

segments.voice: Read that page slowly. Phebe has been "a succourer of many, and of myself also." Then: "Greet Priscilla and Aquila my helpers in Christ Jesus," a wife and husband, her name first, who "for my life laid down their own necks." Then Andronicus and Junia, "my fellowprisoners, who are of note among the apostles." Readers take that last phrase two ways: well known to the apostles, or noted as apostles themselves. In Philippians Paul asks help for "those women which laboured with me in the gospel." And Second Timothy traces a young man's faith back through two women: "which dwelt first in thy grandmother Lois, and thy mother Eunice." That's one side of the letters. The other side is on the page too: "Let your women keep silence in the churches," and, in First Timothy, "I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man." Churches read these differently. Some ordain women as pastors and read the limits as words for particular churches and moments. Others, including the Catholic and Orthodox churches and some Protestant churches, ordain only men as priests or pastors, while honoring women's service in other ways. Whichever way a church reads it, the names stay on the page.
screen: `PHEBE, PRISCILLA, JUNIA.` · `A GRANDMOTHER NAMED LOIS.` · `LIMITS ON THE PAGE TOO.` · `CHURCHES READ IT DIFFERENTLY.` · then, large: `CO-WORKERS IN CHRIST.`

segments.voice: Say out loud the name of a woman who taught you something about faith, or about how to live: a grandmother, a teacher, a neighbor. Let the name sound in the room. Then hold her face in mind for the sit, the way that last page holds Phebe and Priscilla.
Paul and women. Phebe, Priscilla, Junia and others named with thanks in the letters, beside lines that limit women's speaking, which churches read in different ways.
Here's the line: co-workers in Christ, and the last page of Romans is full of them. Sixteen hundred days, and counting.

screen: `DAY 1600 COUNTS.` → `THE LETTERS, READ THROUGH · 69 OF 70.` → `TOMORROW: A LETTER MAILED TO ROME LONG AGO: WHO IS IT ADDRESSED TO NOW?`

howItsDone: Churches read Romans 16 and the letters' lines about women in worship and study, and they differ on ordination: some ordain women as pastors, while the Catholic and Orthodox churches and some Protestant churches ordain only men.

chat.says: grandma's letters keep thanking 'miss ada, who taught me to pray.' pop says nobody remembers her. that's so sad??
options: Then say her name. Paul ends Romans naming women one by one: Phebe, Priscilla, Junia. That's how names get kept.
It's fine. Paul's letters only name the apostles, so ordinary teachers were never meant to be remembered.
It's fine. Scripture remembers the men who taught faith; the women who taught it were left unnamed.
chat.meaning: Paul's last page in Romans names women co-workers one by one, and 2 Timothy names a grandmother, Lois. Saying a name is how it's kept.

Phebe.meaning: a woman Paul commends in Romans 16, a servant of the church

Cenchrea.meaning: the town whose church Phebe served

Junia.meaning: greeted with Andronicus as of note among the apostles

Lois.meaning: Timothy's grandmother, named in Second Timothy

notes: Written 2026-10-13 in the year-2-4 recipe; rewritten 2026-10-15 in recipe v3 (senses shape: a name said aloud carries the idea). Title, word, carry and sources kept; 2 Timothy 1:5 (Lois and Eunice) added; 1 Corinthians 11:5 dropped for length.

The index carry is lowercase ('co-workers in christ') and is kept exactly in the carry field; the voice capitalizes Christ. Suggest capitalizing 'Christ' in the outline. Romans 16:3 KJV says 'helpers'; the Greek συνεργός means fellow worker, which the carry follows.
The KJV spells the names Phebe and Priscilla (Prisca in some verses); the index says Phoebe and Prisca. The script follows the KJV spellings it quotes. Confirm.
'Some readers think she carried the letter itself' (Phebe): a common reading, not stated in the text; framed as 'some readers'. Confirm.
Junia: some later manuscripts and translations read a male name (Junias); the script makes no manuscript claim and gives the two readings of 'of note among the apostles' only. Confirm.

Which churches ordain women is stated broadly (Catholic and Orthodox ordain only men as priests; some Protestant churches ordain only men as pastors; others ordain women). Confirm the wording is fair to all.
Cenchrea is glossed only as the town whose church Phebe served (its location near Corinth is left out under the claims rule).
